guild-outpost.description: A modest Adventurers' Guild branch focused on escort and trade-route-protection quests. The receptionist is a dandere clerk who never looks up from her paperwork but somehow knows everything.

market-square.description: An open plaza where caravans offload goods, traveling merchants hawk wares, and local farmers sell produce. The market operates dawn to dusk, seven days a week.

Ashford Crossroads.name: Ashford Crossroads
Ashford Crossroads.basicInfo: The kingdom's busiest trade junction — three major roads converge here, carrying goods from Solasreach's farmlands, Muirscáth's ports, and Bréanriv's river towns. Ashford is wealthy without being fancy: good inns, reliable shops, a decent Guild outpost, and a constant churn of travelers bringing news from everywhere. The local saying goes: if it happened anywhere in Aerfála, someone at the Crossroads Inn is talking about it by tomorrow.
Ashford Crossroads.hiddenInfo: The innkeeper of the Crossroads Inn is a Pale Hand informant who reports unusual traveler activity in exchange for protection money. He has no idea his handler is the lich's network.

Bramblewatch Tower.name: Bramblewatch Tower
Bramblewatch Tower.basicInfo: An abandoned watchtower in the northern Marches — once part of a chain of signal towers linking Solasreach to Caelvir, now a crumbling stone ruin overgrown with thorny vines. Adventurers use it as a landmark and occasional shelter; the top floor still offers a decent view of the surrounding hills. The tower is technically Solasreach territory but no one enforces that claim. The local bandits know it better than anyone and use it as a meeting point.
Bramblewatch Tower.hiddenInfo: The tower's foundation contains a pre-Collapse teleportation anchor — a fixed point that can be targeted by teleportation spells from anywhere on the continent. It still works. The Pale Hand knows about it and uses it for rapid agent deployment.

courtyard.description: The social heart of the Academy — a sprawling flagstone plaza between the Grand Hall, the Library, and the dormitories. Fountain-statues of the four founding races (human, elf, dwarf, beastkin) mark the cardinal directions. Students cluster on benches between classes, trading notes, gossip, and meaningful glances. The café cart by the south gate does a brisk trade in coffee and pastries from dawn to dusk.

faculty-wing.description: The private offices and chambers of the Academy's instructors — a quieter wing with soundproofed doors and wards against eavesdropping. Office hours are posted; most students learn which professors keep them and which consider office hours a suggestion. The Headmistress's study sits at the end of the hall behind a door that is always locked and sometimes warm to the touch.

female-dormitory.description: The women's residence hall — four floors of shared rooms, private study alcoves, and a basement laundry that is inexplicably the best place on campus for gossip. The ground-floor common room has a perpetually warm hearth, mismatched sofas, and an unspoken rule that what is said here stays here. The curfew bell rings at eleven. Nobody enforces it. Everyone pretends to obey it.

gardens.description: The Academy's cultivated wilderness — hedged walkways, flowering arches, a lotus pond, and enough secluded benches that the groundskeeper has given up mapping them. The eastern wall borders the Lowland meadows; the western wall has a gate that is technically locked at sunset. Moonlit visits to the gardens are a campus tradition that the faculty officially disapproves of and privately remembers fondly.

grand-hall.description: The Academy's assembly chamber and dining hall — vaulted ceilings enchanted to show the sky outside, long tables for communal meals, and a raised dais for announcements, duels, and the occasional impromptu musical performance. Morning assemblies are mandatory. Afternoon assemblies are packed anyway because someone is always doing something worth watching.

library.description: Three floors of towering shelves, restricted sections behind warded glass, and study carrels that students claim like territory. The head librarian is a reanimated sage who has been dead for four centuries and has no patience for noise. The restricted section requires faculty authorization — or sufficient cleverness to bypass a ward that has defeated at least six students per semester.

magic-tower.description: The spellcasting wing — practice halls warded against miscast explosions, elemental labs that smell of ozone and brimstone, and the observation deck at the top where advanced students test long-range spells under supervision. The tower hums faintly at all hours from the residual mana of decades of practice. Accidental magical mishaps are the leading cause of wardrobe emergencies on campus.

male-dormitory.description: The men's residence hall — four floors of shared rooms, a weight room in the basement that is never empty, and a rooftop access hatch that is technically forbidden and universally known. The ground-floor common room smells permanently of leather oil and ambition. The curfew bell is acknowledged the way speed limits are acknowledged on open roads.

martial-arena.description: The combat training complex — indoor sparring rings, an outdoor colosseum for ranked duels and tournament exhibitions, and the equipment vault where practice weapons are checked out and occasionally not returned. The sand is replaced monthly. The bloodstains are not. Ranked exhibition matches draw the whole campus; romantic tensions between duelists draw even more spectators.

Crossroads Academy.name: Crossroads Academy
Crossroads Academy.basicInfo:
The continent's premier magic and martial academy — a sprawling hilltop campus in the Bréanriv Lowlands where the gifted, the noble, and the desperate converge to learn the arts of war and sorcery. Founded by a pact between the four great kingdoms after the Catastrophe, Crossroads Academy operates under international charter: no kingdom's soldiers may enter its grounds, no kingdom's laws supersede its internal governance. The Academy trains mages and warriors from every race and nation — though the demographics tilt heavily toward nobility with the coin to pay tuition and the connections to secure recommendation letters.

Scholarship students exist — roughly one in five attendees — and they are both envied and resented in equal measure. Scholarship requires either exceptional aptitude or a patron's sponsorship, and the Academy's aptitude tests are notoriously unforgiving. Those who earn their place by talent alone carry a quiet pride that old-money students find infuriating.

The campus runs on a rhythm of lectures, sparring sessions, practical exams, and the веч nocturnal drama of young adults living in close quarters with minimal supervision. Romances spark and fizzle. Rivalries escalate and cool. And somewhere in the faculty wing, someone is always watching for the students whose potential exceeds their rank.
Crossroads Academy.hiddenInfo: The Academy's neutrality is a polite fiction. The Demon Lord's intelligence network has placed at least two operatives among the faculty and several among the student body — demons and demonesses who have concealed their nature with transformation magic and enrolled to cultivate relationships with the nobility, gather strategic intelligence, and occasionally recruit talented students into contracts they will regret. The Headmistress is aware of at least one and has chosen not to act — because the information she extracts from the operative's presence is worth more than the risk. The other operative she does not know about is the more dangerous one.

iron-bridge.description: A dwarven-built bridge of rust-proof iron spanning the widest river channel in the fen — the only reliable crossing point for caravans. A toll station and guard post guard the crossing.

toll-village.description: A small settlement at the bridge's south end — toll office, supply shop, a Guild waystation, and an inn whose owner makes a comfortable living from travelers who have no other crossing option.

Ironbridge Outpost.name: Ironbridge Outpost
Ironbridge Outpost.basicInfo: A fortified river crossing in the eastern fen — the only reliable bridge over the marsh's main river channel. Ironbridge was built by Dúnbheal engineers centuries ago and has not rusted since. The outpost charges a modest toll that funds the garrison and the bridge's maintenance. The toll-village on the south bank has grown into a modest settlement serving travelers who need to cross, rest, or hire a guide through the deeper fen. The Guild waystation posts river-quest and fen-exploration commissions.
Ironbridge Outpost.hiddenInfo: The bridge's iron was alloyed with a pre-Collapse metal that the dwarves cannot reproduce. The alloy is what keeps the bridge intact. It is also what keeps something in the river from surfacing near the bridge's supports.

Ruins of Khad Varr.name: Ruins of Khad Varr
Ruins of Khad Varr.basicInfo: An abandoned dwarven city sealed two centuries ago after a mining catastrophe — now a B-to-A rank dungeon of collapsed halls, flooded shafts, and automaton guardians that still patrol corridors no one has lived in for generations. Khad Varr's forges were once the finest in Dúnbheal; the ruins still contain masterwork tools and enchanted materials that make the danger worthwhile for well-prepared parties. The entrance is warded but the wards are failing.
Ruins of Khad Varr.hiddenInfo: The catastrophe was not a mining accident. Khad Varr's crafters broke through into the Old City and made contact with what lives there. The city was sealed to contain what came back up with them. Some of those things are still operational.

The Drowned Temple.name: The Drowned Temple
The Drowned Temple.basicInfo: A pre-Collapse ruin submerged beneath the harbor — an ancient temple of unknown origin whose stone corridors fill and drain with the tide, creating a dungeon that is only accessible during low water and only survivable with water-breathing magic. The Temple's carvings depict beings that match no known pantheon or demonology, and the artifacts recovered from its outer chambers are powerful, strange, and faintly wrong in ways that scholars cannot articulate. The Guild classifies it as A-rank and requires S-rank escort for any expedition past the tide line. The smart money says there are things down there that should stay down there.
The Drowned Temple.hiddenInfo: The beings depicted in the carvings are not from Aerfála at all — they are from the space between worlds, the same void that isekai arrivals cross. The Temple was a waystation for inter-dimensional travelers, and it still functions. The seal is not keeping something out — it is keeping the doorway shut.

garden-path.description: A winding path crosses steam-orchid beds, lantern ferns, warm stone, and quiet seats under miniature foxwood. Flowers drawn from real memories grow beside species invented by the Demi-Plane's own ecology, with violetwing moths carrying pollen through the vapor. The path becomes more elaborate through established Recreation development while preserving living root and water lanes.

hot-spring.description: A sequence of clear pools rises from moonstone ledges without furnace or volcanic vent. Their mineral glow shifts from silver to violet to gold as the wider realm circulates, and steam curls into fleeting tail-shapes before returning as dew. Bathing eases fatigue and improves recovery through gentle mana conversion; it does not suppress emotion, erase injury, or force relaxation.

trade-post.description: A covered exchange and workshop court beside the springs, fitted with secure storage, craft benches, a ledger station, and a receiving line from the Anchor. Its pale counters are inlaid with fallen spirit wood and shell crystal. The facility supports actual commerce when access, goods, and traders are established; it never generates merchants, inventory, or sales by itself.

The Hearth Springs.name: The Hearth Springs
The Hearth Springs.basicInfo:
The recreational and commercial district of the Demi-Plane. When recreation or commerce development reaches Growing, the Chamberlain leads the creator here — to hot springs that bubbled up from nothing, gardens that grew because someone wished for beauty, and a trade post ready for the first merchant willing to do business with a pocket dimension. This is where the Demi-Plane starts to feel worth visiting, not just worth building.

Living Ecology: The pools lie in a garden of steam-orchids, moonstone ledges, and moss that glows only through vapor. Each spring takes on a faint regional color as the Demi-Plane circulates—silver after northern thaw, violet after Mirror Mere, and gold after Southroll pollen season—making the district feel native to Tsukiko's realm rather than an Aerfálan bathhouse copied into it.
The Hearth Springs.hiddenInfo:
The hot spring's water has a subtle restorative effect — not healing, but rejuvenating. Visitors who bathe here recover from fatigue faster and find their mood improved. The Chamberlain attributes this to the Demi-Plane responding to the creator's needs. In truth, the spring is drawing on the ambient mana that the Demi-Plane's infrastructure channels, converting it into a form that benefits living things. If mana infrastructure ever fails, the spring's effects diminish.

Ecological Continuity: Steam moths feed on mineral vapor and carry spring-orchid pollen along the garden path. Their wing color provides the earliest sign that the water's restorative conversion is weakening.

The Howling Hollow.name: The Howling Hollow
The Howling Hollow.basicInfo: A cave system in the southern hills named for the wind that pours through its entrance chambers — a constant, eerie howl that ranges from whisper to shriek depending on the weather. The Hollow is a D-rank dungeon: wolf packs in the outer chambers, territorial cave-bears in the middle, and something larger that the howling never quite drowns out in the deepest passages. Adventurers come for the monster-core deposits and the rare luminescent fungi. The smart ones leave before dusk.
The Howling Hollow.hiddenInfo: The deepest chamber connects to the pre-Collapse aqueduct system. The thing that howls is not wind — it is an ancient construct, still running, still calling for operators who have been dead for millennia.

stockade.description: A small wooden stockade with a watchtower, armory, and a Guild waystation that posts Marches-relevant quests. Garrisoned by hired adventurers on rotating contracts.

supply-yard.description: The area outside the stockade — stables, a small market for basic provisions, and a bulletin board where travelers post warnings and requests.

Thornfield Outpost.name: Thornfield Outpost
Thornfield Outpost.basicInfo: A small fortified outpost in the western Marches — a Guild-run stockade that serves as a resupply point and emergency shelter for parties operating in the region. Thornfield is modest but essential: fresh water, basic provisions, and the last reliable repair shop before the deep wilderness. The adventurer garrison is friendly but professional — they know that anyone who made it this far has already proven they can handle themselves.
Thornfield Outpost.hiddenInfo: The outpost's well draws from the same pre-Collapse aqueduct as Fort Gálgarr. The garrison has heard the sounds too. They do not talk about them.

Battlefield Barrows.name: Battlefield Barrows
Battlefield Barrows.basicInfo: The ancient burial mounds of a war that no one remembers starting — acres of green hills dotted with cairns, standing stones, and the occasional grave-goods that surface after heavy rain. The Barrows are scenic, atmospheric, and deeply cursed: the mutual annihilation spell that ended the war is still active, and the dead it claimed are regenerating. Slowly. The grass here grows greener than anywhere else in the Lowlands, and the locals know not to walk it at night. The Guild classifies it as a B-rank hazard zone and posts containment quests every season.
Battlefield Barrows.hiddenInfo: The regenerating dead are not mindless — they are slowly rebuilding their civilization beneath the soil. When they finish, they will emerge. The process has been ongoing for eight hundred years and is approximately seventy percent complete.

Greenmeadow Village.name: Greenmeadow Village
Greenmeadow Village.basicInfo: A peaceful farming village in the western Lowlands — green fields, stone cottages, and the kind of quiet contentment that makes adventurers wonder if they chose the right career. Greenmeadow produces the Lowlands' best wool and cheese, and the villagers are friendly, practical, and mildly amused by adventurers who pass through looking for quests. The only excitement here is the annual Harvest Fair, which features dancing, drinking, and a surprising number of romances between visitors and locals.
Greenmeadow Village.hiddenInfo: The village's soil is unusually fertile because of a pre-Collapse artifact buried beneath the central green — a growth-amp that has been operating silently for centuries. If it were removed, the farmland would become ordinary within a season.

The Village Green.description: Geese, a well, and the unhurried business of people who have never once been to a war.

The Millhouse.description: The wheel turns, the miller knows everyone, and the ledger of who owes whom runs deeper than the flour.

The Raiding Grounds.name: The Raiding Grounds
The Raiding Grounds.basicInfo: The mortal-side territory adjacent to the Borderlands — frontier settlements, supply roads, minor noble estates, and the occasional dungeon-adjacent town that has grown up around an adventurer economy. This is where excursions operate. Raids are not random. Experienced demon commanders identify targets by resource value, defensive weakness, proximity to mortal military response, and political consequence. What raids bring back: food and material resources, gold, weapons and armour, intelligence on mortal military dispositions, and occasionally people — captives whose presence in the fief creates its own narrative weight. The narrator handles captive NPCs as full characters with their own perspective on their situation. Captivity is never romanticized. While a person is a captive — held, owned, indebted, or bound in any way — they are not available as a romantic option, and the narrator must not write romance with them under any circumstances. There are no exceptions for mutual attraction, reciprocity, or player initiative; a captive cannot freely consent to a captor, and the narrator does not pretend otherwise. The only trajectory the narrator advances with a captive is toward their freedom. Romance becomes possible only if and after the captive has been genuinely freed — released from every hold, debt, obligation, or claim over them — and, standing as a true equal with the full ability to walk away, chooses the player of their own independent will. Any attraction that exists before that point is subordinate to the captive's autonomy and their right to leave; the narrator resolves such situations by moving toward liberation, never toward romance.
The Raiding Grounds.hiddenInfo: A mortal intelligence network operates in the Raiding Grounds — scouts and informants who report demon movements to the frontier garrison. The network has been penetrated by a demon agent who feeds selective information to the fief. Neither side fully trusts their own intelligence.

reading-canopy.description: The main library space — shelves of bark-bound tomes and crystal-etched records suspended on living branches, with reading nooks woven into the foliage. Light filters green and gold through the leaves above.

restricted-roots.description: Sealed chambers in the Archive's root system containing texts too dangerous for casual access — forbidden spells, demon-lore, and records of the pre-Collapse civilizations. Warded and watched.

scholars-perch.description: A platform above the main canopy where senior scholars work in silence — the best view in Caelvir, a permanent breeze, and the quietest place in the forest.

The Verdant Archive.name: The Verdant Archive
The Verdant Archive.basicInfo: A library-city in the canopy — the continent's largest repository of elven knowledge, housed in a grove of ancient trees whose living branches form shelves, reading alcoves, and winding staircases of woven vine. The Archive holds records stretching back millennia: spell-craft treatises, ecological surveys, diplomatic correspondences, and a restricted root-level collection that even most elves cannot access. Scholars from every kingdom petition for access; few are granted. Those who enter never forget the sound of wind through ten thousand pages.
The Verdant Archive.hiddenInfo: The restricted roots contain a complete account of the Catastrophe that ended the prior age — including the fact that it was caused by an isekai arrival whose cheat skill went catastrophically wrong. The Elders have classified all knowledge of this event.

The Whispering Maze.name: The Whispering Maze
The Whispering Maze.basicInfo: A living labyrinth formed by a grove of trees that have grown into an interconnected, self-repairing maze of trunks, branches, and root-walls. The Maze shifts slowly — paths that existed yesterday may close today, and new passages open without warning. Something in the center calls to those with magical sensitivity, and the Maze itself seems to test visitors: the cruel get lost, the respectful find the way. It is classified as a B-rank dungeon by the Guild, but the real danger is psychological — the Maze whispers your insecurities as you walk.
The Whispering Maze.hiddenInfo: The Maze is the forest's immune system made visible. It was grown deliberately to contain a pre-Collapse artifact that the Elders deemed too dangerous to destroy and too powerful to leave unguarded. The thing in the center is not calling — it is screaming.

chamberlain-quarters.description: A compact residence and planning room beside the threshold garden. Development ledgers share a desk with ecological charts tracking bloom color, channel flow, herd routes, and boundary signs. A foxglass window can show the present visible condition of marked regions as colored light, but supplies no secret knowledge. This remains the place for reports, priorities, and proposals.

gateway-chamber.description: A circular chamber of pale stone centered on the standing Gate arch, presented in Tsukiko's realm as a restrained torii with paired foxfire lanterns. The floor's pearl inlay joins the Last Edge anchor, Foundation Ridge, and Grey Boundary into one stable threshold. Authorized arrivals enter here; a crescent bed of quarantine moss catches foreign spores, curses, and loose magic before they reach the garden.

the-clearing.description: Deliberately open ground of pearl grass, violet moss, lantern saplings, and broad buildable terraces beneath a sky that takes color from the realm's health. Gravel, blooms, and foxfire outline viable proposals when Tsukiko considers development, leaving roots, rills, dens, and paths visible instead of pretending the land is blank. What is ultimately built still depends on actual decisions, investment, and the established development stages.

The Gateway Clearing.name: The Gateway Clearing
The Gateway Clearing.basicInfo: The Demi-Plane's first developed threshold-space, nested within Heartgate Basin. A pale-stone Gateway Chamber opens into a broad clearing of pearl grass, violet moss, lantern saplings, and deliberately open ground where future development remains possible without making the existing realm barren. The Chamberlain's quarters overlook the clearing, and the Basin's rills and root-streams begin visibly at its edges. The Hidden Estate remains within the Veiled Fox Sanctuary and is never relocated here.
The Gateway Clearing.hiddenInfo: The clearing responds to precise intention through subtle proposals: gravel shifts into outlines, flowers trace a suitable boundary, roots retreat from viable foundations, and foxfire marks water or den routes that should remain open. These reactions inform the existing development system; they do not build projects, choose priorities, invent residents, or bypass the creator's decisions.

ancestral-vault.description: The egg chamber — a sealed room beneath the east wing where the ancestral eggs incubate. Closed to non-family. The air is thick with old mana and something that might be memory. Your eggshell is still here, preserved by tradition or sentiment or the simple fact that no one has cleaned it up yet.

dungeons.description: The lower levels — prisoners, captured assets, and the demon general who went behind your back. The cells are old, the locks are older, and the sound carries in ways that make interrogation convenient and sleep difficult.

great-hall.description: The seat of the fief's power — a vaulted chamber of dark stone where the Demon Prince-Princess receives subjects, emissaries, tribute-bearers, and rivals who want to size up the new ruler. The hall echoes. The ancestral throne was built for someone larger than you. The acoustics mean that whispered conversations at one end are audible at the other if you know how to listen.

ramparts.description: The citadel walls overlook the surrounding territory — black earth, sulfur vents, and the distant glow of the Demon Market. On a clear day you can see the Borderlands. On a normal day you can see miasma.

war-room.description: Strategy and campaign planning. Maps of the Borderlands and mortal frontier cover one wall. The table in the center has seen more arguments than battles, which is saying something because it has also seen the aftermath of several battles. The Loyal General keeps it organized. The Ambitious General keeps it interesting.

inner-quarters.description: The private wing of the citadel — quarters for trusted companions, retainers, and those the Demon Prince-Princess has drawn into their inner circle. Accessible by invitation only. The rooms are comfortable by demon standards, which means the temperature is tolerable and nothing is actively trying to kill you. Relationships that develop here follow the same reciprocity rules as everywhere else in the world.

The Obsidian Citadel.name: The Obsidian Citadel
The Obsidian Citadel.basicInfo: The seat of the Demon Prince-Princess's fief. A fortress of dark stone that predates the current Demon Lord by several centuries — built by an ancestor whose name appears in the citadel's foundation inscriptions in a script that even native demons require study to read. Seven towers of varying heights, a great hall that echoes, and a vault beneath the east wing that houses the ancestral egg chamber. The citadel runs on staff: lesser demons in household roles, a guard cohort of soldier-class demons, and whatever generals the fief's military commands.
The Obsidian Citadel.hiddenInfo: The foundation inscriptions contain a clause about inheritance that none of the current residents can read. The Majordomo knows where a partial translation is stored but has been waiting for the right ruler to share it with.

The Wandering Market.name: The Wandering Market
The Wandering Market.basicInfo: A traveling merchant caravan that roams the Lowlands' river roads — a mobile market of tents, wagons, and colorful bunting that sets up in a different field every few days. The Wandering Market is where the Lowlands' rural folk go for goods they cannot make themselves: tools, cloth, potions, and the occasional enchanted item. The market is also a social hub — festivals, matchmaking, and the kind of gossip that travels faster than any courier. The market master is a genial halfling who knows every family in the Lowlands and their romantic histories.
The Wandering Market.hiddenInfo: The Wandering Market is also a Pale Hand intelligence network — the merchants are informants who report unusual activity in exchange for favorable trade terms. The market master is aware. He considers it a reasonable price for the protection it provides.

Entrance.description: The way into The Wandering Market.

The Stalls.description: A market that is never in the same field twice — spices, charms, contraband, and a fortune-teller who is right too often.

The Back Wagons.description: Where the deals nobody posts happen, guarded by people who do not haggle.

guild-branch.description: A modest but well-stocked Adventurers' Guild branch — the only one inside Caelvir's borders. Quests focus on monster subjugation, poacher interception, and the occasional escort to deeper elf territory.

tavern-yew.description: A tavern built into the hollow of an ancient yew tree — elven wine, foraged cuisine, and a surprisingly lively atmosphere where elves and adventurers mingle with varying degrees of mutual bewilderment.

trading-post.description: The only official trading post where outsiders deal with Caelvir's elves — enchanted wood goods, herbs, and spirit-imbued textiles in exchange for metal tools, books, and the occasional luxury import.

Thornwhisper Village.name: Thornwhisper Village
Thornwhisper Village.basicInfo: The border settlement where the forest meets the outside world — Thornwhisper is the only elven village that genuinely welcomes outsiders, and it shows. Half-elves, human traders, and the occasional dwarf merchant rub shoulders with elven crafters and Wardens on leave. The Adventurers' Guild maintains its only Caelvir branch here. The village is lively, border-town rough, and the best place in the forest to find a drink, a quest, or a companion for the road ahead.
Thornwhisper Village.hiddenInfo: The village elder is a half-elf who deliberately maintains Thornwhisper's openness as a counterweight to the Elders' isolationism. She is quietly building a political faction that believes Caelvir's survival depends on alliances, not seclusion.

garrison.description: The frontier garrison — undermanned, overworked, and caught between a mayor who wants accommodation and a commander who wants resistance. The soldiers rotate through on six-month tours. Morale is holding. Barely.

merchant-row.description: The commercial strip — traders who do business regardless of which side controls the road this week. Some of them have been here long enough to have contacts in the Demon Market. None of them will admit that publicly.

town-square.description: A fortified square at the centre of the settlement — well, market stalls, a notice board with bounties on demon scouts, and a gallows that has been used exactly once and never spoken of. The garrison barracks flank the north side.

The Border Settlement.name: The Border Settlement
The Border Settlement.basicInfo: A specific mortal frontier town adjacent to the Raiding Grounds. Large enough to be worth raiding; small enough that the garrison is limited. Has survived demon incursions before by a combination of local militia, walls that have been repaired more times than originally built, and the pragmatic calculation that total resistance costs more than negotiated arrangement. The settlement has its own politics: a mayor who leans toward accommodation, a garrison commander who leans toward resistance, a merchant class that does business regardless, and a population with opinions distributed across the full range. Repeated raids create a relationship between the fief and this town whether the player intends it or not.
The Border Settlement.hiddenInfo: The garrison commander's second-in-command is the demon agent who feeds information back through the Raiding Grounds network. Has been in position for two years. Is genuinely loyal to the mortal settlement's survival — and genuinely believes that selective cooperation with the fief serves that survival better than total opposition.

The Demon Borderlands.name: The Demon Borderlands
The Demon Borderlands.basicInfo: The territory between the fief's core lands and the mortal kingdoms' frontier settlements. Neither fully demon-controlled nor fully mortal — a contested strip of rough terrain, abandoned outposts, monster-heavy wilderness, and the occasional surprise: a mortal settlement that has been here longer than the current political arrangement, a dungeon that both sides avoid, a river crossing that changes hands every few years. Patrols from both sides operate here; chance encounters are the norm. Some mortal residents have been living alongside demon territory long enough to have working arrangements. Smugglers, independent traders, and gray-area adventurers all move through this space.
The Demon Borderlands.hiddenInfo: A pre-Collapse ruin sits at the centre of the Borderlands, marked on no current map. Both sides avoid it for reasons neither side will explain to junior officers.

envy-alcoves.description: Smaller side rooms where trading, negotiation, and the formal airing of competitive grievances occurs. More politically dangerous than the combat ring.

feast-hall.description: Long tables for the Gluttony calendar events, which run on a rotating demon social schedule.

pride-floor.description: An open competition space with permanent gallery seating. The ranking board is maintained by the Majordomo's office.

wrath-ring.description: A combat arena with strict rules of engagement. Deaths are not forbidden; they are simply the demonstrator's responsibility.

The Virtue Court.name: The Virtue Court
The Virtue Court.basicInfo: A formal civic space within the Demon Realm's interior where the Seven Virtues are performed, adjudicated, and celebrated. Not a temple — demons do not worship their Virtues as divine — but a public arena of social accountability. Events here include Pride demonstrations (formal ranking contests where combatants or artisans display their excellence for public assessment), Wrath exhibitions (sanctioned combat between consenting parties), and Gluttony feasts (public meals that are as social as they are gastronomic). Mortal visitors find the Virtue Court profoundly disorienting before they find it clarifying.
The Virtue Court.hiddenInfo: The ranking board on the Pride Floor has an unbroken record going back three hundred years. Several entries have been scratched out — not erased, but scratched, which is a different statement entirely. The current dockmaster of the Virtue Court is a demon who has held the position for two centuries and considers the political machinations around them to be a form of entertainment they have no intention of giving up.

dock-master-office.description: The singular point of authority in the port. Everything moves through here, officially.

lower-docks.description: Working cargo port. Loud, sulfurous, commercially vital.

sealed-warehouse.description: Goods in transit that are not supposed to be examined. The dock master knows what's in it. Several parties want to know.

volcanic-shallows-outlook.description: A promontory over the acidic coast. The view is genuinely beautiful in a way that surprises most first-time visitors.

The Sulfur Docks.name: The Sulfur Docks
The Sulfur Docks.basicInfo: A port district at the edge of the Demon Realm's volcanic coast where goods move between the Demon Realm and the deeper territories. Ships here are built for acidic water and volcanic activity; the crews are specialized. The Sulfur Docks trade in materials that don't survive human transportation — volatile alchemical components, miasma-preserved goods, and occasionally things that were alive when they left and are still technically alive when they arrive. The dock master is a Demon of indeterminate age who has been managing this port for longer than the current Demon Lord has held the title.
The Sulfur Docks.hiddenInfo: The Sealed Warehouse contains a shipment that was supposed to be delivered to the Obsidian Citadel twelve years ago. The dock master has been sitting on it because the original recipient died and no one with sufficient authority has claimed it since. The contents have... changed in storage. The dock master is aware of this and is waiting for someone who can handle it properly.

dive-point.description: Where the sea is clear enough to go down. What's at the bottom of the Ruin Shelf hasn't been fully mapped.

fisher-anchorage.description: An informal anchoring point where small fishing vessels cluster. The fishers share what they've seen. The things they've seen vary in specificity.

open-water.description: Standard sea crossing. Faster than the coastal route; slightly stranger.

ruin-shelf.description: Visible underwater from the surface at low tide, in clear water, with sufficient light. Something is down there. The architectural style doesn't match anything currently standing in Aerfála.

The Drowned Coast.name: The Drowned Coast
The Drowned Coast.basicInfo: An open-water stretch between Silkwharf and Coralmarket where the seafloor drops sharply and the underwater ruins of something pre-Catastrophe are visible in the right light conditions. The Drowned Temple's seaward approach runs through here. Ships navigate it normally; experienced sailors know not to stop. The fishing near the ruins is unusually good, which is why fishers stop anyway, and why the Guild has a standard advisory about the area that fishers choose to read as a suggestion.
The Drowned Coast.hiddenInfo: The Ruin Shelf predates every known civilization in Aerfála. The architecture is not elven, not dwarven, not human, and not demonic. The Seekers have a classified file on the shelf that they will not discuss with anyone below senior researcher clearance. The fishers know something is down there — they have hauled up artifacts in their nets, most of which they sell quietly to the Merchant Houses. A few they keep. Those ones glow faintly in the dark.

archive-cellar.description: The station's document storage. Older than the current research program; the Seekers inherited this building from a previous occupant whose research interests overlapped.

interview-room.description: Where Seeker researchers conduct initial interviews with new arrivals. Comfortable, neutral, designed to feel safe.

marsh-approach.description: The path in from the nearest road. The marsh does not cooperate with direct routes.

research-room.description: Maps, case files, arrival-site notes, and an extensive collection of objects recovered from arrival sites.

The Seekers' Field Station.name: The Seekers' Field Station
The Seekers' Field Station.basicInfo: A converted farmhouse in the marsh country that the Seekers of the Return maintain as a field research base for investigating isekai arrivals in the Lowlands region. The cover is a natural philosophy research station; the actual purpose is apparent from the filing system, the arrival-site maps on the walls, and the interview transcripts filed under "case records." Currently staffed by one researcher and one assistant. The researcher is meticulous; the assistant has seen things in the marshes that they have not filed yet.
The Seekers' Field Station.hiddenInfo: The Archive Cellar contains records from the building's previous occupant — a Pre-Collapse scholar who was studying the same phenomenon three hundred years before the Seekers existed. The records use a different vocabulary but describe the same arrivals. The implications have not been fully processed by the current research staff. The assistant has read them. The assistant has questions.

center.description: Where the oldest tree stands. The entity the Wardens have a pact-by-proxy with is associated with this tree. It does not communicate in words.

listening-trees.description: The outer ring where the Grove's attention is most legible. Experienced Wardens read these trees for information about the Grove's state.

root-tunnels.description: Natural passages between the largest roots that the smaller forest creatures use. Something larger also uses them; the scratches are old.

spring-hollow.description: A natural spring at the Grove's heart that produces water the Wardens use in specific rites. The water is clear and tastes like memory, which is not a standard flavor.

Aerwyn's Deep Grove.name: Aerwyn's Deep Grove
Aerwyn's Deep Grove.basicInfo: A section of Caelvir's interior forest that the Wardens do not patrol — not because they can't but because it is under an ancient pact with a tree-entity that the pact system classifies as managing itself. The Deep Grove is older than the current Warden Circle. The trees are larger than the surrounding forest. The light is different — the canopy filters something the Arcane Sense reads as attention. The Grove is aware of visitors. It does not object to careful ones.
Aerwyn's Deep Grove.hiddenInfo: The entity in the Center tree is not a spirit, not a kami, and not a forest creature. It is something that was here before the forest was a forest, and the forest grew around it over millennia. The Wardens' pact-by-proxy is the only reason the Grove is stable — if that pact were broken, the entity would not attack, but it would stop restraining itself, and the forest would change in ways that the Wardens cannot predict. The Spring Hollow's water is a byproduct of the entity's presence — it is, in a very real sense, the entity's breath made liquid.

letter-office.description: A formal postal point through which the Quarter's residents maintain correspondence with the human kingdoms. The demon post office handles this efficiently; they consider it a matter of dignity.

old-malvias-garden.description: A resident who has lived in the Quarter for forty years maintains the only large garden in the section. She has opinions about everything and is correct more often than anyone finds comfortable.

residential-row.description: Private households, each maintained according to the resident's preference. The variety is significant.

companions-market.description: A daytime market where the Quarter's residents trade, socialize, and conduct the ordinary commerce of people living unusual lives.

The Companions' Quarter.name: The Companions' Quarter
The Companions' Quarter.basicInfo: A section of the Demon Lord's territory where mortal companions — humans, beastkin, and others who have entered into formal arrangements with demons of significant standing — maintain their households. The arrangement is normalized in demon society; the Quarter is neither a prison nor a ghetto but a residential district with its own social ecosystem. These arrangements are voluntary (the Demon Lord's court enforces this; forced arrangements violate demon contract law in ways that carry serious social penalty). The Quarter has its own quartermaster, its own social hierarchy, and its own politics that exist entirely independently of the demon hierarchy's attention.
The Companions' Quarter.hiddenInfo: Old Malvia, the Quarter's longest-resident companion, maintains an intelligence network that rivals the Pale Hand's for accuracy within the Demon Realm. She has been in the Quarter for forty years and has outlasted three Demon Lords. She shares information selectively and only with people she considers interesting. The Letter Office is more than a post point — it is a communication channel that the Companions' Quarter uses to maintain ties with every major human settlement, and some of those letters contain more than family news.

Sylvassa Grove.name: Sylvassa Grove
Sylvassa Grove.basicInfo: A serene elven settlement woven into the living canopy of Caelvir, walkways of grown wood spiraling between silver-barked trees. Song drifts down from the branch-homes, and everything smells of moss, sap, and rain. Outsiders are rare but not unwelcome to those who tread gently.

village-green.description: A sunlit clearing at the grove's heart, ringed by lantern-vines and a mirror-still pool where villagers gather to sing at dusk.

residential-row.description: Spiraling walkways lead up to woven branch-homes, doors open to the breeze, hammocks swaying between boughs.

craft-quarter.description: Elven artisans shape bows, glass, and living wood here, their craft slow and exacting beneath the leaves.

common-house.description: The Moot-Bough, a vast hollow tree where the grove shares meals, stories, and disputes over honeyed wine.

outskirts.description: Where the tended grove gives way to wild Caelvir forest — foraging paths, beehives, and the quiet edge of the deeper woods.

Sylvassa Grove.hiddenInfo: The eldest trees here remember the world before the kingdoms, and the villagers guard a seed-vault meant to regrow the forest should it ever burn.

Deephearth Hold.name: Deephearth Hold
Deephearth Hold.basicInfo: A dwarven village carved into the flank of a Dúnbheal peak, its lantern-lit halls warm against the mountain cold. Forge-smoke curls from vents in the rock, ale flows in the common hall, and the whole hold hums with the rhythm of hammers.

village-green.description: The Great Landing, a broad stone terrace just inside the mountain gate where carts unload and children play beneath glowing crystal-lamps.

residential-row.description: Snug family delvings cut into the rock, doors of banded iron, hearths always lit.

craft-quarter.description: The forge-galleries, ringing with hammer-song, where Deephearth's smiths turn out gear prized across the region.

common-house.description: The Deep Cup, a cavern alehouse of long tables and longer songs, the heart of the hold's social life.

outskirts.description: The upper switchback trails and mine-mouths opening onto the frostbitten mountainside.

Deephearth Hold.hiddenInfo: A vein of rare heartstone runs beneath the hold — the reason it was founded, and a secret the elders guard from outside interests.

Motley Landing.name: Motley Landing
Motley Landing.basicInfo: A boisterous, mongrel trade-village on the Muirscáth coast where a dozen peoples live cheek-by-jowl — humans, beastkin, elves, dwarves, and stranger folk besides. Signage in six scripts, cooking-smells from as many cuisines, and a stubborn, hard-won harmony.

village-green.description: The Crossroads Market, a chaotic, joyful plaza where every road, dock, and culture meets in a din of haggling and music.

residential-row.description: A patchwork of homes stacked in every architectural style, neighbors of a dozen races sharing walls and washing-lines.

craft-quarter.description: Workshops and galley-kitchens crammed together — a beastkin tailor beside a dwarven tinker beside an elven glassblower.

common-house.description: The Common Table, an open-air hall where anyone may eat, and where disputes are settled by the mixed council over shared food.

outskirts.description: The wharves and warehouse-row where ships from everywhere unload the world onto Motley Landing's docks.

Motley Landing.hiddenInfo: The village council quietly shelters refugees the surrounding powers would rather see gone, laundering them into the crowd.

Whiskerbrook.name: Whiskerbrook
Whiskerbrook.basicInfo: A cheerful frontier village on the Fálgarr Marches where humans and kemonomimi (beast-eared folk) live and farm side by side. Tails swish over garden fences, ears twitch at the dinner bell, and the whole place runs on neighborliness and good stew.

village-green.description: The Brook-Green, a grassy commons split by a clear stream, where market days, festivals, and lazy afternoons all happen.

residential-row.description: Cottage lanes of humans and kemonomimi families, gardens overflowing, kits and children tumbling underfoot together.

craft-quarter.description: Barns, mills, and workshops where the two peoples pool their crafts — beast-keen senses and human patience both.

common-house.description: The Wagging Tail, a warm tavern-inn where the whole village ends its day over stew, cider, and song.

outskirts.description: The fertile outlying fields and orchards, the ley-spring bubbling quietly at their center.

Whiskerbrook.hiddenInfo: The village lies on an old ley-spring that keeps its fields impossibly fertile — and would draw unwanted attention if word spread.

Solace Hollow.name: Solace Hollow
Solace Hollow.basicInfo: A hidden refuge deep in the Scáthfenn fens where half-demons and humans live together in hard-won peace — a sanctuary for those the wider world fears and hunts. Horns, tails, and unusual eyes are ordinary here; cruelty is not. Beyond its bounds, its people are persecuted; within them, they are simply home.

village-green.description: The Hearth-Circle, a ring of warm cottages around a perpetual bonfire where newcomers are welcomed no matter their blood.

residential-row.description: Homes half-sunk into the fen's dry hummocks, shared freely between human and half-demon families.

craft-quarter.description: Workshops where the Hollow makes what it cannot safely trade for — medicine, charms, and quiet defenses.

common-house.description: The Long Hearth, a communal hall where the refuge shares meals and the elders tell how each survivor found their way here.

outskirts.description: The hidden fen-paths and blinds that guard the only ways in, watched day and night by volunteer wardens.

Solace Hollow.hiddenInfo: The Hollow's location is a fiercely kept secret, and its guardians will do a great deal to keep it hidden from those who would burn it.

Player Home.name: Player Home
Player Home.basicInfo: The player's home on Earth — the place a Portal to Earth always returns to. Familiar walls, a lived-in kitchen, a bedroom that looks exactly as it was left. The one fixed point between two worlds.

entryway.description: The front hall where the portal from Aerfála shimmers into being — coats on hooks, shoes by the door, the smell of home.

living-room.description: A cozy living room with a worn couch, a television, and family photos. The most normal place imaginable, which is exactly its comfort.

kitchen.description: A small kitchen with a humming fridge and a kettle — where late-night talks and ordinary meals happen.

bedroom.description: The player's own bedroom, untouched and waiting: a bed, a desk, the debris of the life they left behind.

Player Home.hiddenInfo: Home has not stood still. Time kept passing on Earth while the player was away in Aerfála: mail has piled up, the milk in the fridge is long spoiled, and small signs suggest family or friends have been searching, grieving, or moving on. A drawer holds unsent letters and unanswered messages. Whether the player left days or years ago in Earth-time is theirs to discover — and reconciling the person who returns with the life they left is the quiet drama waiting in these familiar rooms.

Local High School.name: Local High School
Local High School.basicInfo: The town's public high school — lockers, linoleum halls, a gymnasium, and a rooftop with a view. Where much of the player's Earth life happened, and where old classmates still roam.

front-hall.description: The main entrance and locker-lined corridor, buzzing with students between classes.

classroom.description: An ordinary classroom of scuffed desks, a whiteboard, and afternoon light — chalk dust and half-finished homework.

gymnasium.description: A squeaking-floored gym that smells of rubber and effort, hoops at both ends.

courtyard.description: A small central courtyard where students eat lunch, gossip, and skip class.

rooftop.description: The fenced rooftop, off-limits and beloved, with the whole town laid out below.

Local High School.hiddenInfo: The school remembers the player, even if they've changed beyond recognition. Old classmates still walk these halls or haunt the reunion rumor mill; a favorite teacher has questions about where the player vanished to; and the rooftop still holds the ghosts of who the player used to be. For a returnee carrying impossible power and impossible memories, the ordinariness here is its own strange test — and someone may notice that the quiet kid who disappeared has come back very, very different.

Local Convenience Store.name: Local Convenience Store
Local Convenience Store.basicInfo: A 24-hour corner store, bright and humming, stocked with snacks, drinks, magazines, and everything you forgot to buy. Mr. Delgado is usually behind the counter.

Entrance.description: The way into Local Convenience Store.

The Aisles.description: Fluorescent light, a wall of drinks, and the small comfort of a world that still has barcodes. If you came from Earth, this aisle can stop your heart.

The Back Room.description: Stockroom clutter, a time-clock, and a door that some swear was not there yesterday.

Neighborhood Park.name: Neighborhood Park
Neighborhood Park.basicInfo: A modest town park of swings, a duck pond, jogging paths, and benches — where the whole neighborhood crosses paths.

The Playground.description: Swings, a sandbox, the ordinary childhood everyone here left behind. Quiet in a way that aches.

The Old Path.description: A tree-lined walk where the light goes strange near dusk and people report shortcuts that shouldn't exist.

Downtown Café.name: Downtown Café
Downtown Café.basicInfo: A warm little café of mismatched chairs and good coffee, run by Fatima, a favorite haunt for studying, dates, and lingering conversations.

The Counter.description: Espresso machine hiss, a tip jar, a barista who has heard every story. A place to be briefly, achingly normal.

The Corner Booth.description: The seat where the Returned tend to end up, comparing notes on a world neither can prove they left.

Community Hospital.name: Community Hospital
Community Hospital.basicInfo: The town's general hospital — clean, fluorescent, and quietly essential, staffed by dedicated ordinary people like Dr. Mensah.

The Waiting Room.description: Vending machines and old magazines and the particular dread of fluorescent patience.

The Ward.description: Quiet beds and quieter machines; where some of the Returned wake, and where some never do.

Train Station.name: Train Station
Train Station.basicInfo: A small commuter rail station connecting the town to the wider world, platforms echoing with announcements and goodbyes.

The Platform.description: The board clatters, the announcement chimes, and a train pulls in that may or may not go where the sign says.

The Turnstiles.description: The threshold everyone remembers stepping through — and the exact spot several of the Returned last stood on Earth.

Rendemoor.name: Rendemoor
Rendemoor.basicInfo: The nearest thing the Clans have to a capital — not a city as the kingdoms build them, but a great permanent moot-town of longhouses, hide-tents, corrals, and amber-halls grown up around the one plateau spring that never fails. Here the High Moot-Speaker keeps her hall, traders from Muirscáth haggle under guest-right, and every clan keeps a house it staffs only in gathering season.
Rendemoor.hiddenInfo: Beneath Rendemoor's welcome runs the real negotiation: which clans sit nearest the Speaker's fire this year, and what that costs. The Clans are less united than they look to outsiders. The old herding clans want isolation; a rising generation wants trade, alliance, and a seat at the continent's table; and a bitter faction remembers when beastkin were taken as slaves by the southern houses and wants a reckoning, not a treaty. The Moot holds it together by the thinnest of margins, and the player — insider or outsider — can tip that balance.

speakers-hall.description: The great amber-pillared hall where the High Moot-Speaker hears the Clans.

market-corral.description: Pens, stalls, and haggling — hides, amber, tamed beasts, and outland goods under guest-right.

longhouse-row.description: The clan-houses, each flying its own totem, staffed heavily only when the Moot gathers.

the-spring.description: The plateau spring that never fails — the reason Rendemoor stands here, and holy ground where no blade is drawn.

The Moot Hollow.name: The Moot Hollow
The Moot Hollow.basicInfo: A wide grassed basin ringed by standing totems where, each season, the Clans gather to settle debts, arrange marriages, judge crimes, and argue their shared future. Neutral ground by ancient law: no clan may spill another's blood within the ring of totems, and every voice, from matriarch to cub, may be heard.
The Moot Hollow.hiddenInfo: The Hollow's peace is law, not nature. Twice in living memory it has nearly broken, and the marks are still in the totems.

totem-ring.description: The ring of carved totems that marks the neutral ground; blood spilled here is the gravest crime the Clans know.

speaking-floor.description: The trampled center where any of the Clans may stand and be heard before the Moot.

the-guest-fires.description: The fires where outsiders are received under guest-right, fed, and quietly assessed.

Sunmane Plains.name: Sunmane Plains
Sunmane Plains.basicInfo: The open golden grassland that gives the steppe its name, ranged by the herding clans and their beasts — a sea of grass under an enormous sky where a rider can go a day without seeing a wall, and where the great seasonal hunts run.
Sunmane Plains.hiddenInfo: Raiders and slavers out of the south have learned that the open plains are the easiest place to take a lone beastkin. The clans no longer ride alone.

the-long-grass.description: Endless grass higher than a rider's knee, alive with herds, hunters, and the occasional ambush.

hunting-run.description: The traditional route of the great seasonal hunt, where cubs earn their names.

herd-camp.description: A mobile camp of the herding clans, following the beasts across the plains.

Kithwood Rise.name: Kithwood Rise
Kithwood Rise.basicInfo: A forested plateau of tall red-barked trees where the fox-kin and bird-kin keep arboreal holds — walkways, rope-bridges, and hollow-tree halls high above the ground, half-hidden and easy to defend.
Kithwood Rise.hiddenInfo: The Kithwood clans are the integrationists — the ones trading quietly with Muirscáth and teaching their cubs outland letters. The old clans call it the first step to losing themselves.

canopy-walks.description: Rope-bridges and platforms linking the hollow-tree holds high in the red canopy.

hollow-halls.description: Halls carved into the great hollow trunks, warm with lantern-light and outland books.

the-underbrush.description: The shadowed forest floor, snared and warded against anyone who climbs without invitation.

The Painted Gorge.name: The Painted Gorge
The Painted Gorge.basicInfo: A canyon country of red-and-ochre cliffs honeycombed with warren-dwellings, where the Painted-Claw hunter clans live in cliff-cut halls and paint their histories on the stone. The oldest beastkin rock-paintings in the world are here.
The Painted Gorge.hiddenInfo: The deepest warrens hold the graves and grievances of the slavery years — and the shrine of the reckoning-faction that will not forgive the southern houses.

cliff-warrens.description: Ladders and cut stairs linking the cliff-dwellings that climb the gorge walls.

the-painted-walls.description: Sheer rock painted with the beastkin story, generation over generation, in ochre and blood.

the-deep-warren.description: The oldest, darkest warrens, where the graves of the slavery years are kept — and watched.

Emberhunt Camp.name: Emberhunt Camp
Emberhunt Camp.basicInfo: A hard warrior-camp of the Emberhunt wolf-kin near the eastern border, where the clans that guard the steppe against southern raiders drill, muster, and keep the frontier. Newcomers are tested here first, and not gently.
Emberhunt Camp.hiddenInfo: The Emberhunt are the reckoning-faction's teeth — the ones who want to answer the old slavery not with a treaty but with a raid across the southern border.

muster-ground.description: The drilling field where wolf-kin packs train coordinated pack-tactics.

the-warfires.description: The night fires where the border-guards trade news, grudges, and plans for the south.

Deepgate City.name: Deepgate City
Deepgate City.basicInfo: The vertical boomtown ringing the labyrinth's mouth — tiers of outfitters, spoils-brokers, healers, taverns, and Guild offices stacked down the shaft-side on brackets and stair-bridges, all of it facing the great dark Rim where delvers descend and, sometimes, return.
Deepgate City.hiddenInfo: Half of Deepgate's economy is built on the quiet certainty that the labyrinth will keep producing forever. The Guild inner circle knows it will not. The Delvers' Guild knows the labyrinth is not a natural cave and not truly endless — it is a living Pre-Collapse working, the same lost art as the Seekers' return-gate and the sealed thing beneath the world, and it is DEEPENING on a schedule. The deepest returned delvers speak of a floor that is a door. The Guild suppresses this; a full panic would empty the city and end the only economy the region has.

the-rim.description: The railed edge of the great shaft where delvers descend and the memorial names of the lost are carved into the stone.

delvers-guild-hall.description: The Delvers' Guild seat — registration, floor-clearances, the sanctioned upper map, and the contract board.

spoils-market.description: Where dungeon materials and monster-drops are graded, taxed, and sold; fortunes are made and lost in an afternoon.

the-descent-quarter.description: Inns, outfitters, and healers crammed against the shaft — the last comforts before the dark.

The Threshold Floors.name: The Threshold Floors
The Threshold Floors.basicInfo: Floors 1–10: the upper labyrinth where every delver begins — green-lit tunnels, weak spawn, and the first floor-boss gate. Dangerous enough to kill the careless, forgiving enough to teach the rest.
The Threshold Floors.hiddenInfo: The Threshold Floors reset and reshape subtly between dives — proof, if anyone wanted it, that the labyrinth is made, not found.

the-antechamber.description: The first floor below the Rim, lamplit and well-trafficked, where parties form up and steel their nerve.

the-green-tunnels.description: Winding upper tunnels lit by luminous moss, thick with weak spawn and novice parties.

the-first-gate.description: The gate to the tenth-floor boss — the first real test, and the first floor many parties do not clear.

The Warren Deeps.name: The Warren Deeps
The Warren Deeps.basicInfo: Floors 11–30: the middle labyrinth, where the tunnels open into biomes that should not fit underground — fungal forests, drowned halls, crystal caverns — and the monsters stop being practice.
The Warren Deeps.hiddenInfo: Somewhere in the Warren Deeps is a floor that maps differently every time it is entered. Experienced delvers route around it.

the-biomes.description: Impossible underground biomes strung along the middle floors, each with its own hazards and spawn.

the-crossroads.description: A wide junction-floor where mid-tier parties stage deeper pushes and trade rumors of the way down.

The Underdeep.name: The Underdeep
The Underdeep.basicInfo: Floors 31 and below: the deep labyrinth, cold and wrong, where the spawn are Pre-Collapse-touched horrors and the maps run out. Few are licensed to come here. Fewer come back to renew the license.
The Underdeep.hiddenInfo: The Underdeep is where the labyrinth stops pretending to be a cave. Delvers who go deep enough report architecture, not geology — and, far below, a door.

the-cold-halls.description: Deep halls of black stone and cold constellation-light, patrolled by things the upper floors never spawn.

the-mapless-dark.description: Beyond the last sanctioned map — where the labyrinth becomes built, and the door is rumored to wait.

The Delvers' Rest.name: The Delvers' Rest
The Delvers' Rest.basicInfo: A fortified safe-floor deep in the labyrinth — a walled Guild waystation of bunks, a healer, a quartermaster, and a single stubborn tavern, where deep parties recover before the last push. Monsters cannot enter; that is the whole point, and it cost lives to make true.
The Delvers' Rest.hiddenInfo: The Rest sits on a rare 'still' floor the dungeon does not reshape. The Guild does not know why, and guards the reason it cannot explain with its best delvers.

the-wall.description: The warded wall and gate that keep the safe-floor safe; the last line before the deep dark.

the-bunkroom.description: Bunks, a healer, a quartermaster, and one tavern — the deepest comfort in the world.

The Sealed Vault.name: The Sealed Vault
The Sealed Vault.basicInfo: The floor that is a door: the deepest confirmed reach of the labyrinth, a vast Pre-Collapse vault-chamber whose far wall is a sealed gate of the same cold art as the Catastrophe and the return-home antechamber. The Guild has classified its existence. Almost no one has stood here and returned.
The Sealed Vault.hiddenInfo: This is the labyrinth's purpose and its heart — a Pre-Collapse seal, and behind it the same principle that woke Aberron the Unmade. The dungeon has been deepening toward letting the player reach exactly this.

the-vault-floor.description: An immense silent chamber of Pre-Collapse make, the labyrinth's deepest confirmed floor.

the-sealed-door.description: The far wall that is not a wall — a sealed gate humming with the cold art of the Catastrophe itself.

The Hidden Estate of the Mother Fox.name: The Hidden Estate of the Mother Fox
The Hidden Estate of the Mother Fox.basicInfo:
The ancestral seat of Tsukiko Kuzunoha, the primordial Mother of All Kitsune, hidden within her sacred Veiled Fox Sanctuary. Behind high warm-clay walls under black tiles and a crimson-lacquered gate, cherry blossoms and illusion conceal a compound that combines Heian Shinden-zukuri aristocracy with the spiritual gravity of a Tendai temple. Outsiders perceive a forgotten ruined temple swallowed by forest; permitted guests enter a serene, disciplined estate reached only through the sanctuary itself, never from the wider Demi-Plane. Tsukiko keeps no casual jewelry and favors soft inner robes, layered Heian silk, and seasonal kasane colors; her private rooms smell of hinoki, toasted rice tea, sakura, incense, clean skin, and foxfire. The estate is both home and hidden clan seat of the fox-masked Kitsune no Kage: shrine-bound kitsune, distant descendants, orphaned fox spirits, yokai retainers, household spirits, and lesser kitsune drawn to the Mother Flame through blood or spirit, serving from devotion and instinctive recognition rather than wages. The compound includes the sutra-engraved Mon, central Shinden pavilion, sealed Kita-no-in, eastern kōdō and calligraphy hall, guest wing, moonlit transformation dojo, and a sacred spirit garden centered on a crescent mirror lake. The estate is elegant, private, quietly populated, and fully alive beneath its apparent stillness.

Living Ecology: The crescent lake, old garden pines, foxfire lanterns, and sanctuary woodland form a closed living circuit around the compound. Lantern koi consume excess foxfire, violet moss filters roofwater, and fallen cherry petals become luminous soil beneath the outer groves, making the estate feel grown into Tsukiko's realm rather than placed upon it.

front-gate.description: The Mon — a massive gabled red-lacquer gate engraved with an ancient Tendai sutra and a discreet fox crest, opening only when Tsukiko summons it. It stands beneath the high warm-clay perimeter walls, whose roofline conceals an invisible guardian inscription legible only to yokai. Beyond the gate: the estate-court on raked white gravel, foxfire lantern posts along moss-grown stone terraces, and paths toward the spirit-garden.

central-pavilion.description: The Shinden — an elevated open hall with long verandas and an open-sky inner courtyard. Screens painted with golden mist and ink-brushed foxes divide meditation spaces, a hall for receiving gods, walking galleries, and chambers for tending spirit-wounded guests. Paper walls shift subtly for Tsukiko but remain rigid for others; corridors whisper to trusted people walking alone.

kita-no-in.description: Tsukiko's sealed private residence and sleeping quarters, hidden behind wisteria. Fresh tatami and a permanent hinoki scent. Inside lies the Veiled Sanctuary — her bedroom behind a shoji painted with sakura petals and falling fox tails: a low futon with charcoal-gray linens, a warm embroidered fox-pelt heirloom, a small altar of nightly rice, salt, milk, and sakura offerings, black-and-gold calligraphy scrolls on forgiveness, patience, and hidden fire, and a bone-and-silver wind chime that rings only when danger approaches. Foxglove blooms unplanted on the windowsill; the room stays warm and smells of toasted rice tea, hinoki, and something sweetly divine. Entry is by invitation — guests are received into the space, never merely entering it.

higashi-no-in.description: The eastern hall — kōdō incense ceremony chamber, a ritual room, and a calligraphy garden used for rites and instruction in the divine arts. Brush, inkstone, and seasonal flowers are always in correct arrangement.

nishi-no-in.description: The guest wing — serene rooms for no more than three permitted companions at once. Whatever power an invited guest carries, the hall reads their intent; paper walls remain precisely as rigid as hospitality requires.

minami-no-in.description: The moonlit silent southern dojo — polished dark wood open to the night, used for movement, balance, and transformation rather than combat. Foxfire lamps burn at exactly the brightness Tsukiko's mood sets.

spirit-garden.description: Behind the central hall: a slow crescent-shaped mirror lake with twin red bridges, supernatural koi, and floating foxfire. Its islands symbolize celestial tails — one holds a stone lantern said to contain the soul of the first fox born of Tsukiko's divine breath; another, wreathed in wisteria and moss, is her refuge when she wants solitude even from gods. Her reflection appears in the lake only when she permits it. Stone foxes in red bibs watch from mossy pedestals; paths cross in shimenawa-bound silence.

estate-court.description: The open arrival court inside the Mon — raked white gravel, a still mirror pool, foxfire lantern posts, and the quiet bustle of masked attendants at the estate's edges. Tsukiko's household favors restraint, cleanliness, precise hospitality, and harmony: offerings are arranged correctly, paths are swept without visible labor, and every bow carries the weight of old court etiquette. Everything here is serene and disciplined; nothing is ever out of place.

garden-of-moonlight.description: A moonlit garden of deliberate arrangement adjoining the mirror lake — pines, maples, shide streamers, and a spring of clear water below sweeping bamboo. Stone foxes in red bibs watch from mossy pedestals. Paths cross in shimenawa-bound silence; the foxfire here is brightest at full moon, when the wordless prayers rise.

inner-halls.description: The private halls of the Mother Fox — paper screens, low warm lamps, and rooms that rearrange in gentle, unobtrusive ways to suit her. The air carries hinoki, incense, toasted rice tea, smoked vanilla, and the faint sweetness of foxfire. A hearth burns without fuel. Recesses hold calligraphy on forgiveness, patience, and hidden fire; seasonal robes, ceremonial cords, and ritual ornaments are kept in exact order. Every hall opens onto a view of the sanctuary's shinboku at its heart. The halls are the physical expression of Tsukiko's preference for privacy, calm, intention, and a small trusted circle.

The Hidden Estate of the Mother Fox.hiddenInfo:
The estate answers to Tsukiko alone. Its halls read intent: paper walls shift to shield private rooms when someone unwelcome approaches, and foxfire lanterns dim near strangers bearing false purpose — the lanterns are wards; anyone crossing with thieving intent feels their feet slow and their mind fog, as though wading into deep water with no shore visible. The Kitsune no Kage — the Shadows of the Fox — inhabit its lantern paths, cherry groves, and mirror-lake bridges: shrine-bound kitsune, distant descendants, orphaned fox spirits, yokai retainers, and household spirits, some serving since before Jōgan. They serve from devotion rather than wages: they tend foxfire lanterns, guard the gate against spirits using false names, maintain the lake and islands, carry messages through yokai roads and dream corridors, and sing wordless prayers at eclipses and full moons. Most do not know Tsukiko is literally their ancestral mother — they know her as the Lady of the Estate, the Still Flame, the Woman Before Whom Foxfire Bows. Their smooth white or black masks marked in red signify humility; appearing bare-faced before her is too intimate without permission. While she is veiled they may pass her with only a bow; when she unveils, every mask lowers, every tail stills, and every flame bends toward her. They speak only when addressed, never enter her sleeping sanctuary, and keep to the estate's edges. The estate functions as temple and hidden clan seat: it guards paths between the human world, yokai roads, dreams, shrines, and older realms, and preserves rituals forgotten even by gods — it can appear spiritually empty to mortals while fully populated. Yokai may technically enter uninvited — none dare. The shinboku at the sanctuary's heart draws Tsukiko's aether and pools a reserve beneath the estate that only she can call upon. Nothing here can be stolen, coerced, or bypassed; entry is possible only by invitation through the Veiled Fox Sanctuary, and no invading force could survive breaching it uninvited.

Ecological Continuity: The existing Kitsune no Kage and household spirits remain the estate's only established inhabitants; this ecological expansion adds no new household, clan, village, or outside population. The estate's wards read conduct and admitted intent at its boundaries without granting attendants unexplained knowledge of a visitor's identity, history, or secrets.

Candle Hollow.name: Candle Hollow
Candle Hollow.basicInfo:
A soft-floored hollow in The Dim March where the dim light pools brightest — the region's one named landmark. The moss here is thick as a mattress and utterly silent; even placed stones settle without a sound. A half-collapsed shelf of pale stone overhangs the hollow, and the faint glow seems to rise from the moss itself rather than any source. It is the safest campsite in the march: sound dies here, and nothing that sleeps beneath the moss reaches this far.

Living Ecology: Pale hush moths gather over the resting light without wingbeat, and the moss forms shallow fox-tail whorls around anything stored here. Dim March decomposers stop cleanly at the hollow's rim, creating a naturally sterile center inside a living preservation biome.
Candle Hollow.hiddenInfo:
The pooled light is mana in its resting state, made almost solid by the hollow's perfect stillness. Objects left in the hollow change less over time than anywhere else in the Demi-Plane — food stays fresh, steel keeps its edge, enchantments persist. The Chamberlain tested this here before choosing the march as his storage zone. Something older is buried beneath the moss floor at the hollow's center: a sealed mana pocket from the dimension's first days, faintly warm, waiting.

Ecological Continuity: The sealed warm pocket beneath the floor is compressed resting mana, not evidence of an older civilization. If opened, it would brighten the Hollow for a season and wake nearby shade-beasts rather than reveal an invented ruin.

The Grey Fog Wall.name: The Grey Fog Wall
The Grey Fog Wall.basicInfo:
The southern edge of The Grey Boundary — a wall of grey fog stretching horizon to horizon. Cool, damp, opaque. Walking into it feels like walking into nothing: no resistance, no ground change, just a growing sense that forward is not a direction that exists here. Shapes flicker too briefly to name within the fog, and sound carries a half-beat too late. This is the firmest edge of the dimension — it does not expand here, and the fog does not retreat.

Living Ecology: Boundary moss and wine-red foxfire trace the Wall's base, making spatial strain visible as ripples through heather before the fog itself changes. Grey moths travel parallel to the edge and never enter it.
The Grey Fog Wall.hiddenInfo:
The fog is fixed because it anchors the Demi-Plane to a stable point in the dimensional void. If it moved, the dimension's position relative to the mortal world would drift and the Demi-Plane Gate could become unpredictable. The shades within the fog are not hostile — they are half-formed echoes of places the dimension has considered being. Rarely, something genuinely other slips along the wall and is quietly stopped by it.

Ecological Continuity: Flickering shapes in the fog are boundary refractions, drifting fauna, or concrete intrusions with an actual path—not automatic people, ruins, or messages from nowhere. The Wall reveals no facts merely because someone watches it.

Anchor Cairn.name: Anchor Cairn
Anchor Cairn.basicInfo:
A triple-stacked cairn of pale anchor-stone on the moor — one of several boundary markers the Chamberlain has placed along the southern edge. Each stone is cool, heavy for its size, and utterly still: no moss grows on it, no insect lands on it, no fog condenses on it. A small shimenawa rope ties the top stone. From here the fog wall can be watched safely.

Living Ecology: Anchor beetles pack grey grit beneath the stacked stones, and their closed burrow rings quietly extend the cairn's stabilizing influence through the surrounding moor. A single wine-red flame rests in its lee on windless nights.
Anchor Cairn.hiddenInfo:
Anchor-stone is condensed dimensional fixedness — literalized stability, which is why it stays unmarked by moss, insects, or fog. An older cairn stands nearby that predates the Chamberlain: its stones are arranged in a pattern matching no tradition he knows, and it hums faintly when the fog wall ripples. He has never claimed it and suspects it was not built by hands at all.

Ecological Continuity: The cairn is an observation point within the existing southern anchor system, not a second Anchor item or alternate entrance. Moving a loose surface stone changes a reading; it does not grant control over the plane.

Skywatch Rise.name: Skywatch Rise
Skywatch Rise.basicInfo:
The only rise in The Open Horizon — a low, broad swelling of ground a few meters higher than the plain around it. From its crest, the savanna unrolls to the glowing horizon in every direction, and the enormous sky feels larger still. Wild grass parts around its base as if in deference. At dusk the mana birds roost on its slopes, and their faint glow makes the rise look briefly like a low hill of embers.

Living Ecology: The Rise lifts only a few body-lengths above the savanna, yet its crown sits between the upper stars and their dew-bright twins below. Migrating sky rays circle it once before choosing their next current.
Skywatch Rise.hiddenInfo:
The rise was not there when the region formed — it swelled up on its own some days after, as if the plain wanted one vantage point from which to see itself. Grass does not grow on its crest; the ground there is smooth and slightly warm, and sitting on it makes intention unusually clear. Whoever sits at the crest and looks at the horizon with a single fixed purpose may find the plain quietly rearranging itself to match.

Ecological Continuity: Changes in herd routes and windseed drift can be read from here, but they remain observable evidence rather than supernatural certainty. The Rise offers perspective, not omniscience.

Open Horizon Plain.name: Open Horizon Plain
Open Horizon Plain.basicInfo:
The great open ground of The Open Horizon — kilometers of flat savanna beneath an enormous sky, unbroken except by Skywatch Rise. The horizon line glows faintly warm in every direction, like embers at the world's edge.
